name: Sodalite
physical: Traditionally associated with easing a tense throat and voice
Crystal healers link it with calm, steady breathing
Often kept nearby to support restful sleep
Associated with comfort during stressful periods
summary: Sodalite is the deep blue, white-veined stone of logic and calm, prized by students and speakers. Explore its meaning, care, and how it differs from lapis.
intro: Sodalite is an inky royal blue stone laced with white veins, often mistaken for lapis lazuli at first glance. The difference is that sodalite is a single mineral rather than a rock, and it lacks the golden pyrite flecks of its more famous cousin. Its colour ranges from navy to a lighter periwinkle, and cut pieces show a cloudy, slightly granular depth. Because it is plentiful and affordable, it is one of the most popular tumbled stones and beads. A palm stone feels cool and smooth, and many people find the colour itself quietly settling.
history: Sodalite was first described in 1811 from Greenland, and its name refers to its sodium content. For decades it was little more than a curiosity until a large deposit was found in Ontario, Canada, in 1891. The vivid blue was so striking that the Canadian town of Bancroft supplied it for the decoration of Marlborough House in London, after Princess Patricia chose it for a room, an episode that gave the stone a royal nickname locally. It has since become a favourite for carving and beadwork, and Bolivian, Brazilian and Namibian sources keep supply steady.
meaning: Sodalite is called the stone of logic, and in the crystal tradition it is used to bring order to scattered thoughts. It is associated with the throat and third eye, balancing rational analysis with intuitive knowing. Students keep it nearby to encourage clear study and steady memory, and speakers use it to ease nerves before talking. Emotionally, it is thought to quiet worry-driven mental chatter and to help people state their needs honestly, without drama. In group settings it is believed to encourage trust and shared purpose. Spiritually, it is a gentle meditation partner that helps you notice the difference between fear and wisdom. Many people reach for it when facing a decision that needs both head and heart.
howToUse: Keep a sodalite palm stone on your desk or beside your books during study or exam periods. Hold it while rehearsing a speech or preparing for a tough talk. Place one piece on the brow during a ten-minute meditation, breathing slowly and letting thoughts settle. Wear it as a pendant or bracelet for steady daily support. A small stone on a bedside table is a traditional aid for winding down mentally at night. In a grid, pair it with clear quartz to sharpen focus and with amethyst for a calmer, more intuitive layout.
care: Sodalite is hardy enough for most gentle cleansing. A quick rinse in lukewarm water is fine, but avoid long soaks and harsh chemicals, and dry it thoroughly. Because it is brittle and can chip or cleave, keep it away from hard knocks. Cleanse by smoke, sound, or placing it on selenite, and charge it under the moon. Prolonged strong sun can lighten the colour of some pieces, so a few hours of morning light is plenty. Store it in a pouch away from harder stones.
identify: Genuine sodalite has an even blue body with white calcite or feldspar veining and no metallic flecks. If you see brassy gold dots, it is probably lapis lazuli. Some sodalite is dyed to boost colour, and dyed howlite or glass is sold as imitation, usually with painted-looking veins. Real stone has natural irregularity and feels cool to the touch. Under long-wave ultraviolet light, rare hackmanite-type material can glow orange, but that is a separate variety.

faq.a: In the crystal tradition, sodalite is a stone of logic, calm and honest communication. People use it to support study, public speaking and meditation. These are metaphysical associations rather than medical claims.

faq.q: Is sodalite the same as lapis lazuli?
faq.a: No. Sodalite is a single mineral with white veining, while lapis lazuli is a rock containing lazurite, calcite and golden pyrite. Lapis usually has brassy flecks and a more ultramarine tone, whereas sodalite is plainer and usually cheaper.

A short rinse in lukewarm water is generally safe, but do not soak it for long or use harsh cleaners. Dry it well afterward. Many people prefer to cleanse it with smoke, sound or selenite to protect the polish.
